clue.text: Fed up with the salamander

definitions.meaning: fed up, sick of things, in British slang
a salamander is a kitchen grill or iron plate for toasting the top of a dish, so food treated with it is given a crisp top

explanation.surface: Someone is tired of the mythical fire-dwelling lizard.
explanation.walkthrough: The salamander here is not the lizard but a cook's top-heat grill, which leaves a dish crisp-topped on the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is British slang for fed up and also literally describes a dish finished off under a hot grill.

clue.text: Bread an afterthought of the scholarly

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is the degree of a scholar
PS, postscript, is an afterthought added to a letter

explanation.surface: Some baked goods are added as an extra note by an academic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' is the definition at the front; 'of' makes the scholar's degree come first and the extra note after it.
explanation.definitionFit: These are soft bread rolls, especially in British usage.

clue.text: Father off the dog-lead, look, getting amorous!

indicators.note: off means taken away, so the letters of the parent are removed from the leash

parts.note: dad is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: Dad lets the dog off its leash and starts eyeing someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' takes D, A and D, in order, out of DOG-LEAD, leaving the four other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To leer at someone admiringly is to look at them with amorous intent.

clue.text: The infantry are well versed in it ?

definitions.text: The infantry are well versed in it

parts.words: The infantry are well versed in it
parts.note: infantry here means young children, who know the little verses taught to toddlers by heart

explanation.surface: A claim that foot soldiers are well informed about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Infantry' looks military; it means infants, and 'well versed' is literal, as these are verses.
explanation.definitionFit: Small children learn short traditional verses, so infants are literally well versed in them.

clue.text: Dismal doctor supported by auditor

indicators.note: in a down clue the doctor sits on top of the listener, which holds it up from below

parts.note: an auditor is a hearer, and the organ of hearing is the ear

explanation.surface: A gloomy physician is backed up by an accountant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' looks like an accountant but means a listener.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a poetic form of dreary, meaning gloomy or bleak.

clue.text: Portentous smack

parts.note: portentous means warning of what is coming, and a smack is a flavour, so this is an advance taste

explanation.surface: An ominous slap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' looks like a blow; it means a taste or flavour, and the portent is the 'fore' part.
explanation.definitionFit: An early sample of something to come is a taste that foretells it.

clue.text: Pioneer workers' leader seen in marble in London

definitions.meaning: the prefix ...- means chief, as in archbishop or architect, the leader of builders
Marble ... is a white marble monument at the west end of Oxford Street in London

explanation.surface: The head of a band of pioneers is commemorated in a London marble statue.
explanation.walkthrough: MARBLE ARCH is a London landmark at the end of Oxford Street; the clue's 'in marble' points at the second word of its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Arch- as a prefix means chief or principal, and the landmark's name contains the word.

clue.text: Another abrasive strike — what for ?

parts.note: a match is struck against a rough strip to light it, and striking a second one is done to get the flame going again

explanation.surface: A question about why there is another bitter industrial walkout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abrasive strike' suggests an angry walkout; it is a match scraped on a box, and the second scrape is to set the fire going once more.
explanation.definitionFit: Striking a fresh match is done to kindle the flame again after it has gone out.

clue.text: Flower not found on Cold Comfort Farm

definitions.meaning: the wild pansy, a garden flower

definitions.text: not found on Cold Comfort Farm
definitions.meaning: Cold Comfort Farm is Stella Gibbons's comic novel of a grim farm; ease of heart, comfort, is the thing missing there

explanation.surface: A flower that does not grow on the farm in the famous comic novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Cold Comfort Farm, Stella Gibbons's 1932 novel, mocks gloomy rural fiction; read as two words the flower is peace of mind, which the farm lacks.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an old name for the wild pansy, and read as two words means peace of mind, the opposite of cold comfort.

clue.text: Some speculators are on the top 'of the world

definitions.text: Some speculators are on the top 'of the world

parts.words: Some speculators are on the top 'of the world
parts.note: bears are stock-market speculators betting on falling prices, and the ones at the North Pole live literally on top of the globe

explanation.surface: Certain investors are riding high and feeling on top of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On top of the world' looks like elation; read literally it is the Arctic, home of the white bear, and a bear is also a market speculator.
explanation.definitionFit: Arctic white bears share a name with market speculators who sell expecting prices to fall, and they live at the planet's northern pole.

clue.text: Every inch-45 of them — a woman

definitions.note: a woman's first name, as in the jazz singer Fitzgerald

parts.note: an ell is an old English cloth measure of forty-five inches

explanation.surface: A woman is described as a lady every inch of her, all forty-five inches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every inch' looks like praise of the woman; it begins the description of an old unit, the ell, which held forty-five inches.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a common female first name, so it stands for a woman.

clue.text: In Old Bailey first aid kit ?

definitions.text: In Old Bailey first aid kit

parts.words: In Old Bailey first aid kit
parts.note: the Old Bailey is London's central criminal court, so a sticking plaster kept there would belong to the court

explanation.surface: A question about the contents of the medical box at the famous criminal court.
explanation.walkthrough: The Old Bailey is London's Central Criminal Court. The answer is an old name for a sticking plaster of silk coated with isinglass.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an old adhesive dressing for small cuts, and a dressing kept at a law court would be its plaster.

clue.text: What helps to make a hen cackle ?

definitions.text: What helps to make a hen cackle

parts.words: What helps to make a hen cackle
parts.note: a cheerful idea would make a hen laugh, and the forked breastbone of a fowl, pulled for a wish, carries the same old name

explanation.surface: A question about what could amuse a chicken enough to set it clucking.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the old name for the wishbone of a bird; split into its two words it is a jolly notion, the kind that would make a hen laugh.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an old name for a fowl's wishbone, part of the hen itself, and literally a happy idea that provokes laughter.

clue.text: He demands the tin before he does the job

definitions.text: He demands the tin before he does the job

parts.words: He demands the tin before he does the job
parts.note: tin is slang for money, and a worker in the white metal needs the metal itself before he can begin

explanation.surface: A tradesman insists on cash up front before starting work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tin' looks like slang for money, payment in advance; literally it is the metal this craftsman works.
explanation.definitionFit: A tinsmith, a worker in tin and other light-coloured metals, needs his metal before he can work.

clue.text: Swiss resort to suit Wordsworth, Southey, and' Coleridge

definitions.meaning: a town in the Bernese Oberland between Lakes Thun and Brienz

definitions.text: to suit Wordsworth, Southey, and' Coleridge
definitions.meaning: these were the Lake Poets of the English Lake District, so a place among lakes would suit them

explanation.surface: A Swiss holiday town is said to suit three English Romantic poets.
explanation.walkthrough: The three were the Lake Poets; the Swiss town's name means between the lakes.
explanation.definitionFit: The town's name is Latin-derived for between lakes, and it lies between two, apt for poets named after lakes.

clue.text: Creatures that by a rule in nature teach The act of order to a peopled kingdom"

definitions.text: Creatures that by a rule in nature teach The act of order to a peopled kingdom

parts.words: Creatures that by a rule in nature teach The act of order to a peopled kingdom
parts.note: a quotation from Shakespeare's Henry V, where the Archbishop of Canterbury describes insects in a hive as a model of an ordered state

explanation.surface: A line of verse about creatures whose instinct shows a nation how to govern itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The lines come from Canterbury's speech in Henry V, Act 1 Scene 2, which goes on to describe the hive's king, officers and soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's passage is about hive insects, whose ordered colony is offered as a pattern for a well-run kingdom.

clue.text: Oil's necessary

definitions.meaning: an aromatic oil extracted from a plant is known by this adjective, so the word describes the oil

explanation.surface: Oil is a must.
explanation.definitionFit: A volatile plant extract is called an essence oil by this name, and the word also means indispensable.

clue.text: Less than somewhat early, Milton's primrose

indicators.note: less than the full word, so one letter is dropped from the end of it

parts.note: rather means somewhat, as in rather cold

explanation.surface: Milton's primrose is described as arriving a little early, but not quite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less than' drops the final R from RATHER. Milton's Lycidas has 'the rathe primrose that forsaken dies', using the old word for early-blooming.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an archaic word meaning early or soon, used by Milton for a spring flower that blooms ahead of others.

clue.text: Prepareth to drive, by gum !

definitions.meaning: a golfer sets the ball on a peg before driving, and the old verb ending -eth turns that action into a word in biblical style
these are set in the gums of the mouth, and 'by gum' is a mild oath

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned golfer readies a tee shot and exclaims in mild surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By gum!' reads as an exclamation; literally it says what sits beside the gums. The first part reads TEE-ETH, archaic 'he tees up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as TEE plus the old -eth ending it means places the ball for a drive; and the mouth's biting parts are rooted in the gums.

clue.text: Tearful aboard, those that have been given the brush-off

annotationWithheld.why: Tearful aboard, those that have been given the brush-off: WEEPING inside SS, but 'aboard' alone supplies both the SS and the container signal, one word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Tearful aboard, those that have been given the brush-off

clue.text: Rex Wiseman's waxy with Flora

definitions.note: flora means plant life, standing for one plant here

parts.note: the wise King (Latin rex) of Israel was Solomon, so this is his possessive
a seal is a stamp pressed in wax

explanation.surface: A clever king is said to be cross with a woman called Flora.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waxy' looks like British slang for angry, and Flora like a woman; the seal is pressed into wax, and flora is plant life.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a woodland plant with arching stems and hanging white flowers, so a member of the flora.

clue.text: Perhaps just silly in a way like christopher

definitions.note: Christopher Sly is the drunken tinker in the opening of Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, so this means in Sly's manner

indicators.note: in a way signals the letters of the daft word are rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: Someone is described as rather foolish, like a man called Christopher.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Sly is the tinker in the induction to The Taming of the Shrew; the adverb means in the manner of Sly, and is an old spelling of slyly.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher's surname was Sly, so behaving in his manner is acting cunningly.

clue.text: Weakened spirit of the old admiralty

definitions.text: Weakened spirit of the old admiralty

parts.words: Weakened spirit of the old admiralty
parts.note: rum diluted with water was issued to sailors by order of Admiral Vernon, nicknamed Old ... for his coat

explanation.surface: The morale of the former naval command has been weakened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' looks like morale; it is rum, watered down for sailors on the orders of Admiral Vernon in 1740.
explanation.definitionFit: It is watered rum, the drink named after an eighteenth-century admiral who ordered the dilution.

clue.text: A bit of a boot might raise it

definitions.text: A bit of a boot might raise it

parts.words: A bit of a boot might raise it
parts.note: a kick from a boot raises a red ridge on the skin, and the same word is the leather strip joining a shoe's upper to its sole

explanation.surface: A small kick could leave a mark.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is both a strip of leather in a boot and the raised mark a kick leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: It names a ridge on the skin from a blow and also the leather strip stitched round a boot's sole.

clue.text: Black as the founts of Reading?

definitions.text: Black as the founts of Reading?

parts.words: Black as the founts of Reading?
parts.note: printed reading matter flows from the black fluid of the pen and press, and the Berkshire town of Reading hints at a printing works

explanation.surface: A question about how dark the fountains in the town of Reading are.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading looks like the English town; it is the activity, whose source is the dark fluid that letters are printed or written in.
explanation.definitionFit: Something as black as the dark fluid that pens and printing presses use is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Where the Spanish Main begins?

parts.note: a cape in north-west Spain whose name is Latin for land's end, the point where the open sea, the main, begins

explanation.surface: A question about where the pirates' Caribbean coast starts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spanish Main was the Caribbean coast of Spain's American empire; here 'main' is simply the ocean, which starts at Spain's cape whose Latin name means end of the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: The cape's name comes from Latin for the end of the land, and the main is an old word for the open sea.

clue.text: Voter and helper sought in marriage

definitions.meaning: a vote by show of these counts each raised one
a farm worker or labourer is a helper
a suitor asks for a woman's one of these in marriage

explanation.surface: A voter and an assistant go courting.
explanation.definitionFit: A show of raised palms counts votes, a labourer is a farm helper, and a suitor asks a father for his daughter's in marriage.

clue.text: God, were Jaques to expand his metaphor

definitions.text: God, were Jaques to expand his metaphor

parts.words: God, were Jaques to expand his metaphor
parts.note: Jaques in As You Like It says all the world's a stage; if so, the Creator is the author of the drama

explanation.surface: A suggestion that a Shakespearean character might extend his famous figure of speech to include the deity.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaques's speech beginning 'All the world's a stage' makes men and women players; pushed further, the one who wrote the drama would be God.
explanation.definitionFit: If the world is a stage, the being who devised its drama is its dramatist.
